6.t: Working with data: time in each phase
q: Calculate the mitotic index of each tissue.
Estimate the time an onion root tip cell spends in interphase and in metaphase.
Interphase 180 / 200 × 24 = 21.6 h. Metaphase 4 / 200 × 24 = 0.48 h (about 29 minutes).
State the assumption behind your answer to question 2.
The cells are at random, unsynchronised points in the cycle, so the fraction of cells in a phase equals the fraction of the cycle spent in it.
Explain why the tumour has a much higher mitotic index.
Mutations in oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes remove the normal controls on the cell cycle, so cells divide repeatedly.
Suggest how a mitotic index could help doctors.
To grade a tumour (how fast it is growing) and to see whether a treatment is slowing division.

17.t: Working with data: smoking and lung cancer
q: Calculate how many times greater the risk is for the heaviest smokers than for those who never smoked.
Describe the relationship between cigarettes smoked and death rate.
A dose–response relationship: the more cigarettes per day, the higher the death rate.
Explain how smoking can lead to lung cancer.
Tar contains mutagens that cause mutations in lung cells. Mutations that activate oncogenes or disable tumour suppressor genes can let a cell divide uncontrollably and form a tumour.
Explain how the data for people who stopped smoking support the idea that smoking causes cancer.
Removing the cause lowers the risk (40 against 78 or more), which is what we expect if smoking is a cause, not just linked to it.
Explain why this study alone cannot prove causation, and name one other kind of evidence.
It is observational: smokers may differ in other ways. Other evidence: chemicals in tar cause tumours in animals and mutations in cells; the same pattern is found in many countries.

21.t: Working with data: cancer and age
q: Calculate how many times higher the colon cancer rate is at 80+ than at 40–49.
320 / 15 = about 21 times.
Explain the pattern for colon cancer using oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes.
Several mutations are needed in one cell: activated oncogenes and inactivated tumour suppressor genes. These accumulate over decades, so the chance that one cell has them all rises steeply with age.
Testicular cancer and childhood leukaemia do not follow this pattern. Suggest why.
They need fewer mutations, or some arise before birth or are inherited; they occur in tissues with rapid division at that age (blood cells in early childhood, testes after puberty).
Explain why rates are given per 100 000 people in each age group.
The age groups contain different numbers of people, so rates allow fair comparison.
Suggest why colon cancer screening is usually offered only after about age 50.
Below 50 the rate is low, so the costs and risks of screening (false positives, procedures) outweigh the benefit; most cases occur later.
